Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, died after being ejected from the roller coaster on October 12, prompting an investigation by Cobb County Police and the Georgia Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner.

Nine roller coasters across Six Flags properties remain temporarily closed as the company reviews safety procedures; independent engineers are evaluating findings for the company's more than 220 operating coasters.

During the annual Halloween Fright Fest last Friday, visitors returned to Six Flags Over Georgia, although Goliath remained closed while authorities continue examining evidence regarding the fatal incident.

The coaster's most recent inspection on March 16 reported no violations, though separate reports noted bushings needing replacement, as more than 100 people seek legal representation over injuries allegedly linked to various rides.
title: Six Flags says it will install seat belts on Georgia roller coaster after rider’s death

summary: Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities, triggering disruptions across global government websites this week, according to seven cybersecurity professionals.

Operators have rushed to fix software, with some taking sites offline preemptively, though ArmorCode senior principal solutions engineer Ramy Rahman noted that "more disclosed vulnerabilities do not automatically mean more successful attacks."

This week brought disclosures regarding Node and Plex vulnerabilities, as Virginia-based RunSafe Security CTO Shane Fry warned that "the timescale for not only finding vulnerabilities, but how quickly adversaries can weaponize them" is fundamentally changing.
title: AI-discovered bugs may soon trigger fresh disruptions, cyber experts say

summary: Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to last year, as Americans grapple with high living costs and surging chocolate prices.
Global cocoa prices reached a record high of $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025, driven by poor weather in West Africa and market disruptions from the war in Iran.

Chris Costagli, a vice president at NielsenIQ, said high gas prices averaging $4.29 have worsened affordability concerns, noting "I can't afford it this year because I've paid so much more for so many other things."

title: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns

bias: The left framing makes smiling a conversational wellness practice, using “cracking a smile,” “positivity,” friendship-building, and campus or workplace initiatives to stress social and institutional benefits.

summary: Regular smiling can improve mood and health , research reveals. Dr. Judy Ho, a Los Angeles clinical and forensic neuropsychologist at Pepperdine University, discusses smiling as a coping strategy that affects cortisol and stress levels.

Studies support the 'facial feedback hypothesis,' suggesting physical changes like smiling can alter emotional states. Jeanne Tsai, a psychology professor at Stanford University, notes that smiling during tasks may reduce physiological stress responses.

Cultural perceptions of smiles vary significantly. While some Americans view excited grins as friendlier, some East Asians characterize them as 'emotionally unstable,' Tsai said, illustrating that emotional values differ across cultures.

Retailer Target faced backlash last year for mandating employee smiles and eye contact within 10 feet of customers. Nicholas Coles, an assistant professor at the University of Florida, says people dislike losing 'emotional autonomy.'

Authenticity remains key to any benefit. Coles explains that smiling works best when 'authentic and voluntary,' while Ho suggests a smile can signal care in difficult conversations, serving as a personal interaction tool.
title: Smiling May Improve Mood and Health, Researchers Say

summary: Washington, D.C. and Los Angeles are advancing plans for automated subway lines, seeking to modernize transit infrastructure despite fierce debate over safety risks and substantial upfront costs.

The 2009 Fort Totten crash, which killed nine, paralyzed automation efforts for years before recent system upgrades restored proficiency, Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority CEO Randy Clarke noted.

Los Angeles is reviewing an automated line beneath the Santa Monica Mountains, while Honolulu Skyline project director Vance Tsuda reports the three-year-old system has not recorded a single crash or injury.

International president John Samuelsen of the Transport Workers Union criticized automation as "a catastrophe waiting to happen," citing risks of passenger self-evacuation in systems using third rails.

Metro plans to run driverless Red Line trains by 2033 under a nearly $1 billion investment, which Reason Foundation senior managing director Baruch Feigenbaum said could signal to other cities that automation is viable.
title: Some US transit systems weigh whether to run trains without a human at the controls
